analysis.one_liner: Caps how thoroughly dry-cleaning solvent spills must be cleaned up, limiting costs for cleaners and property owners.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: after being split among four House subcommittees in June 1997, no committee ever acted on it and it expired when the 105th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would set a nationwide ceiling on cleanup of dry-cleaning solvents in soil, groundwater, and surface water: no federal, state, or local agency or court could require anyone doing dry cleaning — or the owner of the land or building — to clean beyond one-tenth of the workplace exposure limit set for solvent fumes under the OSHA law. Governments could still clean to a stricter level, but only at their own expense, and federal drinking water standards would be untouched. The bill was referred to three House committees, then to four subcommittees, and never came up for a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners of dry cleaning businesses and owners of land or buildings where dry cleaning happens. They would gain a hard ceiling on cleanup liability for solvent spills, no matter what state law, local ordinances, or a court would otherwise demand. The bill's own findings say cleanup requirements are inconsistent and fall hardest on small businesses and landowners.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Dry cleaners and commercial property owners

how_it_helps.text: Caps the cleanup level any agency or court could require of dry cleaners and property owners at one-tenth of the workplace exposure equivalent for dry-cleaning solvents, in soil, surface water, groundwater, and other media.
Sets one uniform national ceiling, replacing the state-by-state and site-by-site cleanup demands the bill's findings call inconsistent and conflicting.
Declares in statute that the capped level is 'fully protective of human health,' which would shield owners from further remediation demands based on site-specific evidence.

analysis.who_pays: People who live near solvent-contaminated sites, especially those who drink groundwater, would bear the health risk of solvent left in soil and water at levels above the cap. Taxpayers would bear the cost of any deeper cleanup, because the bill says governments may remediate further only 'at its own cost and expense.'
analysis.who_pays_short: Neighbors of contaminated sites, and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The ceiling is borrowed from a workplace standard designed for healthy adult workers on eight-hour shifts — not children, pregnant women, or residents exposed around the clock. Converting that limit to a one-tenth residential cleanup standard has no scientific basis for protecting people living at a site.

It would cap what courts and agencies can require even where contamination threatens drinking water, and would transfer the cost of any stricter cleanup to taxpayers, since governments may go deeper only at their own expense.

By declaring the capped level 'fully protective' in statute, the bill would substitute a legislative number for site-specific health assessments, foreclosing stricter requirements where evidence warrants them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would deliver real, certain savings to a specific group: dry cleaners and landowners whose cleanup liability can dwarf the value of the business or property. But the way it sets the ceiling is the problem — it converts an occupational fume limit into a residential cleanup standard by a rule of thumb, and then declares the result protective by statute. The costs would fall on neighbors left with solvent in their groundwater and on taxpayers asked to fund any stricter cleanup themselves. As health protection, it is a poorly designed tradeoff; as liability relief, it is straightforward and one-sided.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in four House subcommittees for the rest of the Congress without ever getting a hearing or vote, and died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Rep. Joe Barton of Texas introduced the bill on May 22, 1997, joined by eight original cosponsors from both parties.
The House referred it the same day to three committees: Commerce, Transportation and Infrastructure, and Education and the Workforce.
In June 1997 the bill was split among four subcommittees — Health and Environment, Finance and Hazardous Materials, Water Resources and Environment, and Workforce Protections.
No committee or subcommittee ever took it up again; the action record shows no markup, hearing, floor vote, or further movement before the Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the existing cleanup rules for solvent contamination stayed in force. Communities near dry-cleaner sites kept their full legal protections, while dry cleaners and landowners gained no cap on their cleanup liability.

for.name: Joe Barton
for.what_they_did: Sponsored and introduced the bill capping solvent cleanup requirements.

against.name: House Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Chairs of the committee of first referral
against.what_they_did: Sent the bill to a subcommittee and never scheduled a markup or floor action; the bill died there.

against.name: Transportation and Infrastructure and Education and the Workforce Committees
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill after referral beyond sending it to subcommittees.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship leaned heavily Republican — 71 Republicans to 23 Democrats — and because no vote was ever taken, there is no record of how the full House or Senate would have split.

industries.note: The bill caps their cleanup liability for solvent spills no matter what state law or a court would otherwise require. The savings come from leaving more solvent in soil and groundwater near the shops and their neighbors.

Owners of land or buildings hosting dry cleaners face solvent cleanup liability under existing law; a hard federal ceiling would shield them, with any stricter cleanup pushed onto governments and taxpayers.
A nationwide cap on required remediation of dry-cleaning solvents would reduce downstream liability tied to their products' spills.
Their work exists because cleanup laws mandate it; a statutory ceiling on how clean a site must be would shrink demand for remediation along with the public's protection.
